title: Lesson 3.3 — Phonological Awareness and Tolman's Hourglass
source: User-provided WGU D669 Lesson 3.3 text and resource links
learning_objective: Explain phonological awareness and its relationship to phonemic awareness, the alphabetic principle, and reading development.

concepts.definition: Recognizing and manipulating sound structures in spoken language, including words, syllables, rhyme/onset-rime and individual phonemes; can be taught without print.
examples: Count words in a spoken sentence
Clap syllables in a spoken name

concepts.definition: A subset of phonological awareness: hearing, identifying, blending, segmenting, and manipulating individual phonemes in spoken words.
examples: Replace /m/ in mat with /s/ to say sat

concepts.definition: Instruction in correspondences between written letters/letter patterns (graphemes) and speech sounds (phonemes).
examples: Link the written letters sh with /sh/
Read a printed unfamiliar word using spelling-to-sound relationships

concepts.definition: Understanding that graphemes represent phonemes; supports decoding and encoding.
Using grapheme–phoneme correspondences to access a word's spoken form from its spelling; supports word learning and reading.

tolman_hourglass.overview: A visual model connecting broad phonological awareness to specific phoneme awareness and the alphabetic principle, then expanding into orthographic knowledge and fluent word recognition, spelling and comprehension.
tolman_hourglass.teaching_message: Instruction becomes increasingly precise about speech sounds and then integrates this knowledge with print. It highlights the need for systematic, developmentally appropriate teaching; no single stage represents an absolute age cutoff.
tolman_hourglass.note: This is an instructional paraphrase of the supplied description, not a verbatim recreation of Tolman's diagram. Treat phonological and orthographic knowledge as interconnected, not necessarily a rigid one-way sequence.

source_terms.supplied_definition: a conceptual model that illustrates how broad, general knowledge is progressively filtered and refined into specific, goal-directed behavior through the stages of learning and decision-making
source_terms.context_note: In this literacy lesson, it is used for phonological-to-phonemic-to-orthographic skill connections.

source_terms.supplied_definition: the ability to recognize and manipulate the sounds of spoken language, including words, syllables, and phonemes (individual speech sounds), without necessarily understanding the meaning of the words

reflection_questions: Why is phonological recoding important for reading and writing?
How does the alphabetic principle relate to phonemic awareness?
How do phonological and phonemic awareness prepare students for decoding?
